extracted.intended_audience: computational-humor researchers, HCI/AI researchers, affective computing and human-robot interaction communities
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and desiderata for designing, implementing, and assessing computational systems that produce, detect, or use humor (including jokes, laughter, irony) across modalities and applications. Emphasizes data, multimodality, context-sensitivity, performance/delivery, and application-relevant outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to make jokes (comedians)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems whose goal is to make people amused — producing jokes, riddles, puns, and other humorous texts/utterances (e.g., Jape, HAHAcronym).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by comparing outputs to human-produced jokes (e.g., children’s joke books), measure amusement in human raters. Note the distinction between content-generation and performance systems (some systems rely on human-provided scripts and focus on delivery). Use generation patterns and formal templates (puns, acronym reinterpretation, creative variations) as productive approaches. Anti-pattern: assuming that formal theory automatically yields high-quality comedic performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and generating laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems must recognize laughter (separate speech from pure laughter; voiced/unvoiced; speech overlaid with laughter) and generate appropriate laughs when interacting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition: use acoustic feature batteries (eGeMAPS) and combine with visual cues; distinguish spontaneous vs acted laughter. Generation: strategies include laughing in response to external stimuli, qualified imitation of interlocutor laughter, and learning-based policies that condition on situational variables and partner responses. Evaluate via annotated laughter databases and user studies of perceived appropriateness/infectiousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of irony in interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony implemented via ideational reversal where intended meaning arises by negating a chosen element of literal meaning or pragmatic import.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark ironic elements with multimodal signals (exaggerated/understated language, prosody, gaze, facial expression, gesture). Choice principle: use irony to signal agreement with an emotive user statement by repeating with an inversion signaled as ironic. Evaluate on perceived naturalness, pleasantness, likeability, and appropriateness in context. Anti-pattern: applying irony without adequate multimodal cues or contextual grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context sensitivity and appropriateness of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor placement must be sensitive to situational and user context because humor can have positive or negative effects depending on who the user is and the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish contexts where humor increases likeability/engagement from contexts where it undermines persuasion, trust, or causes offense. Use user modeling and context-aware ML to decide when to use humor. Evaluate by measuring effects on persuasion, acceptability, brand reactions, and differential responses across demographic groups. Anti-pattern: inserting humor uniformly or 'out of place' without user/context differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pervasive humor vs self-contained episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity to exhibit pervasive humor that pervades interaction and personality (rather than isolated set-piece jokes) and to take up interactional opportunities to joke or laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model styles of humor tied to personality traits; design systems to opportunistically inject humor when appropriate. Recognize mastering blends and contingencies is complex and not just a midpoint between comedian and humorless agent. Evaluation should probe longitudinal/coherent behavior across interactions, not only isolated jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quantity, quality, and labeling for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine learning approaches require large quantities of reliable, labeled data reflecting people’s responses to humor (jokes, tweets, captions, laughter annotations, multimodal corpora).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use and build annotated datasets (e.g., HAHA 30,000 annotated tweets, large text corpora, ILHAIRE laughter datasets, New Yorker caption corpora). Beware that restricted or biased datasets may lead to non-human-like solutions; labeling must capture affective responses and contextual signals. Consider language/cultural diversity. Anti-pattern: assuming small or poorly-labeled corpora suffice for modeling pervasive humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodality and perceptual grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is not purely verbal; non-verbal modalities (gesture, posture, gaze, facial expression, prosody, visual context) play crucial roles and are often interchangeable with verbal signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop multimodal perception and generation capabilities; integrate modalities when detecting amusement and when producing irony/comedic effects. Note difficulty in implementing theories for cartoons, slapstick, or multimodal video humor when only verbal descriptions of objects are used. Evaluate with multimodal corpora and user studies; anti-pattern is treating modalities as simply additive or ignoring non-verbal cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications and integration into larger systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor must function as part of a broader application (chatbots, virtual agents, games, educational systems, artificial companions) and cannot generally be detached from overall competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess usefulness case-by-case. Monitor how humor shapes user expectations about other capabilities; evaluate long-term engagement, user satisfaction, and functional outcomes. Ensure fallback/human support where needed. Anti-pattern: adding humor to increase friendliness without ensuring supporting competences, leading to user disillusionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: An agent’s humor must cohere with a consistent character/personality (gender, age, education level, sense of humor) across queries and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and maintain a stable personality profile; when chatbots are deployed, teams commonly tune responses to preserve consistency (human-in-the-loop scripting/editing). Evaluate consistency across interactions and contexts; ensure humor style aligns with the agent’s persona. Anti-pattern: inconsistent humor that conflicts with the designed character, undermining user trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and delivery (comedic timing and embodiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery factors (timing, performative gestures, eye contact, audience interaction, reprise, applause elicitation) and embodiment (robot vs software agent) materially affect comedic success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance systems include staples like opening gestures, reprises, audience-targeting, and elicitation moves. Detect audience amusement and use prompts to select topics. Evaluate live performance dynamics and audience responses; consider differences required by physical embodiment (robots) versus virtual agents. Anti-pattern: focusing only on content while ignoring delivery mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for humorous outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Filters and heuristics to choose likely-amusing outputs, e.g., contrast in meaning (contrast/semiotic opposition), closeness of punning sound to original, familiarity, concreteness and imageability of descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement checks like HAHAcronym’s semantic contrast, Hempelmann’s pun closeness measures, and Jape’s familiarity/concreteness/imageability rules. Use these as ranking/scoring criteria when producing multiple candidates. Evaluate by testing which filters correlate with human amusement ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics and subjective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess systems using subjective and objective measures: amusement, likeability, naturalness, pleasantness, style, appeal, perceived animation/empathy, persuasion, trust, acceptance, and interaction time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human-subject studies, preference comparisons (e.g., children’s ratings for jokes), task-based outcomes (persuasion success), and behavioral metrics (interaction length). Beware that some measures vary by user subgroup; report heterogeneity (gender, identification with victims in pranks, personality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter intensity and acoustic/visual feature correlates
rubrics_metrics.description: Human judgments of laughter intensity depend on acoustic and visual features such as voicing, duration, harmonic structure, and pitch-related measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling intensity, include features for voicing, duration, harmonic content, and pitch; consider that high-intensity laughs may carry intrinsic meaning while low-intensity laughs derive meaning from context. Evaluate intensity perception with annotated datasets and perceptual studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing spontaneous versus acted laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Important classification target: spontaneous laughter differs acoustically and visually from acted laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine eGeMAPS acoustic features with visual information to improve discrimination. Use annotated multimodal datasets like ILHAIRE to train and validate models. Consider implications for downstream interpretation of user state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-in-the-loop development and creative oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-resourced systems rely on human teams to monitor, craft, and develop response patterns, treating agent persona and humor as creative artifacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain human curation for personality consistency and to manage edge cases; this practice is common in major chatbot deployments. Evaluate the extent of human involvement and its effects on perceived quality. Anti-pattern: over-automation without appropriate human oversight leading to inconsistent or inappropriate humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive shaping of humor through learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Using machine learning (including reinforcement learning) to adapt an agent’s humor and social behavior based on user feedback and situational signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement adaptive strategies for when to laugh, when to use irony, and what humor style to adopt (e.g., Weber et al., Piot et al.). Evaluate by measuring improved appropriateness, acceptance, and desired social outcomes; ensure models are trained on representative, well-labeled interaction data. Anti-pattern: applying adaptive learning without clear objectives for desirable outcomes, risking unintended behaviors.
